reviews.reasoning: The two-verse span holds together on tier-1 grounds: the tefillah-le-Moshe title sits inside MT 90:1 alongside the psalm's own opening line, and 90:2 completes the eternity statement before 90:3 pivots to human mortality as a fresh subject. The dual-cite arithmetic (web:Ps.90.0 = oshb:Ps.90.1, web:Ps.90.1 = oshb:Ps.90.1) is correct: MT verse 1 carries both the superscription and the dwelling-place line as one verse, confirmed from the source bytes. The genre-label claim (tefillah + le-Moshe, the book's only Moses title) checks out against the device inventory (le_moshe = [90] only). One defect: the rejected_alternative field curly-quotes WEB text ("You turn man to destruction") but cites only a bare "90:3", not an inline web: ref, breaking the mandatory quote+ref convention in that field.

reviews.reasoning: 90:3-6 forms one address unit: every verse in the span is predicated of Yahweh in the second person (turning, sight, sweeping away) with no addressee change through the grass metaphor's close at 90:6, and 90:7's causal ki (for) opens a fresh clause structure on the far side of the span. The timescale (90:4) and grass (90:5-6) images both illustrate the transience theme 90:3 announces, so declining to split them is defensible. WEB quotations verified verbatim against the source; the span tiles exactly.

90:7 opens with ki (for), confirmed from the source bytes, tying the wrath theme to the preceding transience images as a causal connective. The span runs through the seventy/eighty-year lifespan total (90:10) to the wisdom petition at 90:12, and 90:13 opens its own fresh imperative (Relent, Yahweh) rather than continuing 90:12's reflective request — a legitimate seam. Quotations verified verbatim; boundary_evidence_refs correctly extends one verse past the span's own end to cover the seam it argues.

The closing petition opens on shuvah ("relent/return"), a fresh imperative confirmed byte-true against the source, distinct from 90:12's reflective close. The shuvah/shuvu echo back to 90:3 is correctly labeled tier-2 (verbal-root echo, not a driver), and the cross-span mention of 90:3 is properly mirrored into boundary_evidence_refs. The imperative sequence (satisfy, make glad, let appear, establish) runs consistently addressed to Yahweh through 90:17's doubled closing request with no addressee break.

91:1's participle yoshev (dwells) names a generic third-person figure, and 91:2 turns to first-person confession (web:Ps.91.2: “I will say...my refuge...my God, in whom I trust”) with WEB's own quotation marks closing inside the verse. The direct second-person address that governs the rest of the psalm has not yet opened at 91:2, so grouping these two verses before it begins is sound. Hebrew quote verified byte-true; span tiles exactly against Psalm 91's opening.

The second-person address does run continuously from 91:3 through 91:10 (danger catalogue, then premise-and-result at 91:9-10), and the seam choice against splitting at 91:9 is defensible on its own stated ground (91:9-10 supplying reason and result rather than a new topic). But the substrate-signal claim that the addressee is carried "by second-person suffixed pronouns rather than a fresh independent pronoun" across the span is not accurate: 91:9 opens on the independent second-person pronoun attah, not a bare suffix. If anything that independent pronoun supports the span's own reading of 91:9 as a marked restatement of the refuge premise — it just contradicts the specific grammatical claim offered for it.

reviews.reasoning: The angelic-guardianship image is real and does organize 91:11-13 as a recognizable unit running to the lion-and-serpent triumph before Yahweh's first-person oracle opens at 91:14, so the span itself is defensible on thematic grounds. But the grammatical warrant offered for it is wrong: the rationale and its substrate signal both call "his angels" the span's own grammatical subject, when in the Hebrew clause it is the fronted direct object of a 3ms verb whose subject ("he") continues the referent established across the address (most recently explicit as Yahweh at 91:9). The new element at 91:11 is the object/referent (angels), not the grammatical subject.

reviews.reasoning: The voice shift at 91:14 is real and strongly marked — WEB's own quotation marks open at 91:14 and close at the psalm's final verse, and the Hebrew first-person verb va'afalltehu confirms a divine first-person speaker addressing the trusting individual in the third person. But the substrate signal overstates the case: it calls that first-person verb "unlike the third-person and second-person verbs of the rest of the psalm," when web:Ps.91.2 already carries first-person verbs, opening “I will say” and closing “in whom I trust”, in the psalmist's own confession. The real distinction is not first-person-only-here but a change of SPEAKER — psalmist at 91:2, Yahweh at 91:14 — which the span does not state.
